ratings.rationale: Fabricated emissions are spoofing and can create false targets. Established terrestrial ADS-B demonstrations support E2 at most, discounted for analogue evidence. Commercial RF equipment supports T1p. Cross-checking can expose inconsistencies, but W3 permits undetected deceptive reports; footprint-wide reception bounds affected users.
ratings.issue: The cited satellite-applicability paper may not establish operational LEO exploitation. Distinguish fabricated targets from false positions broadcast by genuine aircraft.

ratings.rationale: Rebroadcasting genuine messages creates stale observations attributable to an aircraft, making spoofing primary and replay-induced data tampering secondary. Terrestrial ADS-B research supports the general mechanism, not equivalent satellite outcomes. Consequences depend on track association and timing; a single aircraft is the conservative affected-user estimate.
ratings.issue: Replay overlaps fabricated-emission spoofing but is distinct by using genuine recorded content. The record does not establish that every replay produces displacement or evades freshness and consistency checks.

ratings.rationale: A genuine aircraft broadcasting an incorrect self-reported position is primarily tampering with reported data, secondarily spoofing its asserted location. The independent localisation should reveal disagreement, but W3 allows a missed verdict. Cited evidence could not be verified, so support is conservatively E0.
ratings.issue: The record conflates deliberate avionics modification with GNSS-induced deception. Its claim that a chain masks the discrepancy lacks a specified mechanism and is not established by the supplied evidence.

ratings.rationale: Interference that prevents valid reception is denial of service, not falsification. ADS-B interference research supports the general mechanism, but terrestrial evidence is only analogous to orbital reception. RF monitoring or loss-of-measurement checks can identify degradation at L1; the footprint defines the likely scope.
ratings.issue: The record does not distinguish detectable loss of reception from interference that resembles ordinary coverage degradation. Its stated footprint impact does not establish constellation-wide denial.

missing_threats.title: GNSS or PTP clock manipulation
missing_threats.why: Clock bias directly contaminates TOA observables and can propagate into position errors; timing manipulation merits a distinct tau threat.

missing_threats.title: Payload measurement tampering
missing_threats.why: Compromised extraction firmware or measurement processing could alter TOA, FOA or AOA independently of the aircraft's broadcast content.

missing_threats.title: RF reception obstruction
missing_threats.why: Antenna faults, front-end saturation or unintentional interference can degrade observability without constituting deliberate in-band jamming.

rubric_ambiguities: The evidence rubric does not define how peer-reviewed terrestrial attack demonstrations map to E1 versus E2 when satellite-specific hardware is absent.
Affected users may mean aircraft, ATM consumers or geographic coverage; the rubric mixes aircraft counts with footprint-based scope.
Discoverability lacks an explicit predicate for replay freshness, so its detection layer depends on unspecified association and tracker checks.
W2 and W3 govern single-satellite clock bias, not necessarily fabricated targets, replay or incorrect aircraft self-reports; applying them to these threats is an extrapolation.
batch_comments.overall: The four records describe distinct mechanisms, although the first three overlap in their potential to create deceptive tracks. Satellite-specific evidence and downstream detection assumptions are insufficiently established. The most important gaps are timing integrity, payload measurement integrity, and explicit separation of fabricated targets, replay, and false self-reported positions.
